record.original_question: Among all plane regions of width 1 that can be moved through a right-angled hallway of width 1 by continuous rigid motions in the plane, which region has the largest possible area?

evidence.quote: Problem 2. Determine the plane region S (from now on and in this section we will call it sofa) of largest area which can be “moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width one” (see below).

Formally, for a parameter t representing time and varying in a closed interval I, we need to find a uniparametric family of rigid motions in the plane Φt such that (1) for every t ∈ I “the sofa is inside the hallway” (Φt(S) ⊂ H) and (2) “the sofa moves continously and without teleportation through the corridor”.

The sofa needs not to be convex. For instance, the shape of the better known solution (its area is approximately 2.2195) reminds to an old telephone (see Figure 4). It was proposed by J. Gerver (see [14] for a precise description) and it is conjectured to be the optimal sofa.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let H ⊂ ℝ² be the L-shaped hallway of unit width formed by the union
  H = {(x,y) : x ≤ 0, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1} ∪ {(x,y) : 0 ≤ x, -x ≤ y ≤ 1 - … } 
more precisely, H = ((-∞, 1] × [0,1]) ∪ ([0,1] × (-∞, 1]), i.e., two perpendicular corridors of width 1 meeting at a right-angled corner.

A "sofa" is any connected planar region S ⊂ ℝ² (not required to be convex) for which there exists a closed interval I ⊂ ℝ and a continuous one-parameter family {Φ_t}_{t ∈ I} of rigid motions of the plane (each Φ_t an orientation-preserving isometry, with t ↦ Φ_t continuous in the usual topology on the group of rigid motions) such that:
  (i) for every t ∈ I, Φ_t(S) ⊂ H;
  (ii) for sufficiently early t the region Φ_t(S) lies entirely in the horizontal corridor (-∞, 1] × [0,1], and for sufficiently late t it lies entirely in the vertical corridor [0,1] × (-∞, 1].

Determine the supremum of the area of S over all such sofas, and exhibit a region attaining it. In particular, decide whether the maximum is achieved by Gerver's region (a specific shape composed of 18 analytic arc pieces with area approximately 2.2195).
artifact.status_search_result: In November 2024, Jineon Baek posted a ~119-page preprint claiming a proof that Gerver's sofa (area ≈ 2.2195) is optimal. The result has been widely reported but, as of early 2026, peer review has not been confirmed as complete in the available sources, so the problem is best described as having a recently announced (not yet fully verified) solution.

status_evidence.title: Optimality of Gerver's Sofa
status_evidence.snippet: Jineon Baek, December 2024 preprint claiming Gerver's sofa attains the maximum area.
status_evidence.claim: A claimed proof of optimality of Gerver's sofa was posted in late 2024.

status_evidence.title: Mathematicians Solve Infamous 'Moving Sofa Problem'
status_evidence.snippet: Baek's proof has yet to undergo thorough peer review, but initial comments from mathematicians seem optimistic.
status_evidence.claim: The proof is announced but pending full peer review.

status_evidence.title: Moving sofa problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Gerver constructed a sofa with 18 curve sections of area approximately 2.2195.
status_evidence.claim: Gerver's lower bound and the conjecture context are standard.
